profile.reading: This Dickens County, Texas site near the small community of Afton is mapped under the name Argo Data Center, reflecting its original developer, but the facility has changed hands and changed purpose since that name was current. Argo Blockchain, a publicly traded Bitcoin mining company, opened the site in May 2022 as an immersion cooled mining facility on a 160 acre campus, running more than 50,000 servers submerged in dielectric fluid at up to 180 megawatts of operating capacity. In December 2022, Argo sold the facility, known as Helios, to Galaxy Digital for approximately 65 million dollars, alongside a 35 million dollar secured loan and a two year hosting agreement, as Argo worked through a period of financial strain. Galaxy Digital has since redeveloped Helios into what it describes as its flagship high performance computing data center campus, pivoting the site from cryptocurrency mining toward artificial intelligence and HPC workloads. The campus has grown to more than 2,200 acres, and in January 2026 Galaxy completed additional ERCOT interconnection studies that secured approval for another 830 megawatts, doubling the campus's total approved power capacity to more than 1.6 gigawatts. Power is delivered through utility AEP Texas, with transmission interconnection provided by Wind Energy Transmission Texas, and Galaxy has signed a long term lease with CoreWeave covering the first phase of the AI buildout, with initial power for that phase expected in early 2026. Galaxy describes the campus infrastructure as built around 100 percent uninterruptible power supply with battery backup, rack densities in the 130 to 140 kilowatt range suited to dense AI server clusters, and multi terabit network connectivity offering sub 15 millisecond latency to Dallas. Galaxy has also announced an on campus emergency services partnership with Total Safety to support operations at the site. At the time of the 2022 sale the site employed roughly 40 people managing day to day operations, a workforce that has presumably grown alongside the much larger AI and HPC buildout now underway. What began as a mid sized cryptocurrency mining operation under Argo Blockchain, at up to 180 megawatts on a 160 acre footprint, is therefore now one of the largest announced AI and HPC data center campuses under development anywhere in Texas, spanning more than 2,200 acres under Galaxy Digital's ownership, a scale and purpose shift the Argo era name on this record does not reflect.

The OSM name 'Argo Data Center' is outdated (reflects pre-Dec-2022 ownership) but the site itself is real, current, and highly notable. reading.body:
The Helios campus spans 2,200 acres in Dickens County, Texas, with Galaxy Digital's published approval for 1.6 gigawatts of total power capacity. In January 2026, Galaxy completed interconnection studies that secured an additional 830 megawatts on top of its prior 770-megawatt approval. The campus was originally built by Argo Blockchain as a Bitcoin mining facility running up to 180 megawatts, then acquired by Galaxy Digital in December 2022 and repurposed toward AI and HPC workloads. Power is delivered by AEP Texas through Wind Energy Transmission Texas.

At 140 kilowatts per rack, a common AI cluster density, 1.6 gigawatts of available IT load translates to roughly 11,400 racks capable of hosting dense accelerator clusters. Galaxy has signed a lease with CoreWeave for the first phase, with initial power expected in early 2026. The campus operates with 100 percent uninterruptible power supply and battery backup, and offers sub-15-millisecond latency to Dallas through multi-terabit network connectivity. These specifications qualify the campus to host high-performance compute and AI training workloads requiring dense power delivery and low-latency network access.

Helios ranks 19th among published-capacity facilities in Texas, but this ranking reflects only the 18 other facilities in the state that have published specifications. Texas shows 133 mapped data center locations with a published total of 468 megawatts across all 18 reporting facilities. Helios alone represents 1.6 gigawatts of approved capacity, making it substantially larger than the entire published base in the state by more than a factor of three, though this comparison involves only those sites whose operators have disclosed specifications.
